en: Prosperity! The Viśvaprakāśa, composed by the eminent scholar Śrī Maheśvara.
Homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Let us praise the supreme physician who brings an end to the afflictions of great delusion.
To the All-Knowing One, who understands the causes of the three realms, for the sake of the destruction of suffering. || 1 ||
Upon the blossomed lotus of the heart, [I place] the seal of a drop of nectar from the play of artistic grace.
I bow to that goddess Sarasvatī, who delights in fashioning [the world] for the poets.
The moon arising from the root of the joy of the lilies that are the lords of poets.
It is radiant with the moonlight of an intellect that rivals the wisdom of Vācaspati. || 3 ||

I pay homage to the Guru, who is worthy of worship by the entire world and the unique Rohaṇa mountain for the jewels of his virtues; he whose glory and splendor shine forth like the garland of waves from the agitated Ocean of Milk.
Bearing the unique position of a wave arising from the ocean of the faultless medical science of King Śrī Sāhasāṅka.
He whose conduct was as beautiful as the moon, named Haricandra, adorned the Caraka-tantra with his own commentary. || 5 ||
In his lineage, which was worthy of worship by kings whose dominion was limitless, there was one who was the crest-jewel of all medical arts.
Like the two Dasras to Śakra, so was Śrī Kṛṣṇa to the lord of Gādhipura—a canopy for the spreading creeper of his stainless fame.
The ocean of thousands of disputants, agitated by the fire of the eon consisting of the chatter of numerous conceptual constructions born of mental volition;
His son was Dāmodara, who possessed the three eyes of the three-fold logic and was the most excellent among physicians for those afflicted by disease.
To him was born a son of noble speech, who delighted in the beauty of the goddess of eloquence, Vācaspati.
The illustrious Daṇḍin is the sun to the lotus of the science of good physicians, and the moon to the white lilies of the virtuous.
And his brother Keśava, having attained the glory of being a veritable ocean of jewels of all the principles of medical science, became [famous].
The glory of whose face is skilled in the composition of an elaborate array of words, which serve as the standard for faultless verses and are the abode of fame.
And to Kṛṣṇa was born a son, whose fame was like the pollen of the white lotus, surpassing the splendor of a white parasol.
Śrī Brahmā, whose face is the unimpeded *ātman*, is one whose Sarasvatī is moist with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) made to dance by the radiance of the *bindu* at the tip of his nose. || 10 ||
His son was the illustrious Maheśvara, renowned as a lord among poets, whose fame was as lovely as a fresh white water-lily.
Having reached the further shore of the great ocean of all speech and fear, he became like the white sun for the lotus-pond of the scriptures of grammar. || 11 ||
He whose glory and dignity were attained through the excellence of his skill in composing great literary masterpieces, such as the *Sāhasāṅkacarita* and others.
He who is the sun to the lotus of the three branches of medicine, and the moon to the night-blooming lily grove of virtuous poets.
This is the work of that Great Lord, an ocean of ingenuity among the Supreme Persons.
May the Lord, whose chest is adorned with the Kaustubha gem, shine eternally within the lotuses of our hearts until the end of the kalpa.
Having somehow obtained these excellent jewels of the treasury, which are like the precious gems found in the hands of a master goldsmith, through his skillful artistry.
This fragment of a face, bearing the splendor of a golden band and known as the Viśvaprakāśa, has been fashioned here by me. || 14 ||
Of those eager to churn the ocean of the treasury of words uttered by the lords of the earth.
Why should this golden mountain, which illuminates the universe for the lords of the gods, not be resorted to? 15.
Of those preceded by Bhogīndra, Kātyāyana, Sāhasāṅka, Vācaspati, Vyāḍi, and others.
Of those who possess all forms, who are stainless and auspicious, whose limbs are beautiful, and who are protected by Bhāgura; || 16 ||
This very person, whose priceless qualities are esteemed due to his manifest power, has emerged from the treasury.
How could it not fulfill the desired objects of poets, who are like wish-fulfilling gems? 17.
Whatever exists here, from Mount Mitrashaila and the Western Mountain (Asta) to Mount Ekalavya, Kailāsa, and the circle of the earth;
O wise lords of poets, let all this collection of jewels of words, gathered together in one place beyond [ordinary] reach, be beheld by you. 18.
If you have the desire to churn the great ocean of speech, or if you have the curiosity to attain the station of the Lord of Serpents;
By constantly studying this *Viśvaprakāśa*, may one attain the glory of being a supreme master of grammar. 19.
I have relieved the burden of the accumulation of books for virtuous people.
By composing this wonderful and complete instruction on names, [the author has achieved a marvelous feat].
Resplendent with the successive sequence of one, two, three, four, five, and six syllables.
This compendium of various meanings is being expanded by means of groups such as "the beloved" (kāntā) and others. || 21 ||
In all cases, the various meanings ending in the nominative case are first demonstrated here at the beginning.
It is well-ascertained as occurring within words ending in the seventh case. || 22 ||
In some cases, along with the example, the locative case denotes the substratum alone.
For the sake of clarifying the distinction between genders, there is some repetition here. (23)
The Kaikaka.
Who is the Brahman within Brahmā, the Self, the Wind, the Sun, the Fire, and that which is named "all"?
And in fire, in peacocks, and in water that is pleasant to the head—what [is there]? (24)
The pair of verses.
Akaṃ, pāpe, and duḥkhe are used in the senses of "king" and "country," respectively.
The word *vaka* may refer to the vaka flower, a crane, Śrīda (Kubera), or a Rākṣasa. || 25 ||
*Śuka* refers to the son of Vyāsa, a parrot, and the minister of Rāvaṇa.
The word *śuka* may refer to the *granthiparṇa*, the *śirīṣa*, or sometimes to the *śoṇaka*. (26)
The word *dvika* refers to both a crow and a ruddy sheldrake; *sṛj* refers to an arrow, wind, and a blue lotus.
The word *arka* refers to the sunflower (*arkaparṇa*), rock crystal (*sphaṭika*), the sun (*ravi*), copper (*tāmra*), and the lord of heaven (*divaspati*). || 27 ||
*Karka* refers to the zodiac sign Cancer, a white horse, a mirror, or a water-jar.
Reasoning (tarka) is proclaimed among the various types of action as doubt, deliberation, and pride. || 28 ||
The word *śloka* refers to fame and a verse; the word *loka*, however, refers to the world and people.
*Stoka* means "a little" (*alpa*), and *toka* refers to both a young Cātaka bird and a son (*putra*). || 29 ||
Koka is [the name] for a wheel, a wolf, and the date-palm tree and a frog, when associated with Jyeṣṭhā.
*Ro* is used in the sense of shining; *roka* refers to a hole, as well as a single purchase and a division. || 30 ||
Veka was skilled at roasting and Cheka at capturing trusting deer and birds.
Reka occurs in purgation, in apprehension, and also in vomiting.
The word *kāka* may refer to a crow, a species of tree, or a type of ascetic (pīṭhasarpi).
[The term *śirovakṣālin* refers to] a specific type of person and a particular kind of lamp. || 32 ||
The word *kāka* may denote the *kākanāsā* plant, as well as the plants *kākolī* and *kākajaṅghā*.
In the red variety, it is known as *kāyā*, *malapvā*, and *kākamācī*. || 33 ||
The *kāka* [mudrā] occurs in the binding of women for sexual pleasure, as well as in the gathering of crows.
The root *pāc* is used in the senses of "infant," "old age," "completion," "cooking," and "moistening. || 34 ||
*Śāka* refers to another continent, power, and two specific types of trees.
*Śāka* refers to potherbs and *harītakī*; *nāka* is used for heaven and the intermediate space. || 35 ||
*Mūka* is used for one who is mute or lacking in intellect; *śūka* is used for a mean person, a porcupine, and a horn.
*Bhūka* refers to a hole in the ground and to time; *bheka* refers to a frog and a cloud. || 36 ||
But one [type] alone is exclusively superior, while the other is like something to be spoken of [as inferior].
*Śauka* refers to a flock of parrots and also to a particular part of the female organs. || 37 ||
The word *aṅka* denotes a place, proximity, a mark, a metaphor, a lap, and a characteristic.
In the sections on the Nāṭikā and others, as well as in the Citrayuddha and Bhūṣaṇa; || 38 ||
*Kaṅka* is known as a name for a deceptive bird, for a sword, and for Yama, the god of death.
The word *vaṅka* may denote the part of a saddle and a fragile river-basin. (39)
The word *ṭaṅka* may denote a variety of the *kapittha* fruit, a particular measure, or a pickaxe.
Kope is in Kośa; Jaṅghā is in Ṭaṅkaṇa; and Grāvadāraṇe is in [the same]. || 40 ||
*Raṅka* refers to a wretch or a wrestler; *paṅka* refers to mud or sin.
*Nyaṅku* refers to a deer, a sage, or a mountain; *nāku* refers to a rat, a mountain, or a sage. (41)
*Śaṅku* refers to a peg, Śiva, a sharp point, a number, and a type of arrow.
*Kalka* means a wicked person, sin, hypocrisy, excrement, and filth. (42)
*Valka* refers to the bark; *khaṇḍa* means a piece; *śalka* and *śakala* both mean a splinter or chip, as do *valka* and *śalka*.
*Śulka* refers to what is to be paid at a ferry-crossing and the like, as well as to the dowry given to the bridegroom. (43)
In one hundred and eight gold coins, there are [the values of] dīnāras and kārṣāpaṇas.
It is used as an ornament for the chest, as a golden vessel, and also as a measure of gold weighing one pala.
The word *muṣka* refers to the scrotum, a collection, liberation, and a foot.
*Kiṣku* refers to a span measured from the tip of the thumb to that of the little finger; it also denotes the hand and the forearm, as well as something contemptible. (45)
There should be a *trika* on the rim of the *trikākūpa*, and three *trikas* on the three parts below the back.
And in Laṅkā, the city of the Rākṣasas, among the branches [of the lineage], the Śākinīs, and the unchaste women. || 46 ||
Śaṅkā means fear or doubt; rākā refers to a specific river.
And on the days of the new moon, the full moon, and the full-moon night of the month of Kārttika. || 47 ||
The Kātrika.
*Kanaka* refers to the *campaka*, gold, the *kiṃśuka*, and the *nāgakeśara*.
It is also considered by some to be found in *dhuttūra*, *kāñcanāra*, and even *kālīya*. || 48 ||
The word *karakas*, however, may refer to a skull, a pomegranate, and a water-pot.
*Karakā* refers to a species of bird, the hand, and also to hailstones.
*Naraka* refers to hell or a demon; *saraka* refers to a vessel for liquor.
And [the word] *sīdhu* is used for an uninterrupted line of travelers and for the drinking of liquor. || 50 ||
*Khanaka* refers to one who knows the reality of the mind, a thief who breaks through walls, and a mouse.
Janaka was the dowry for the two royal sages in that age of doubt.
The word *yautaka* refers to a woman's dowry or personal property; *calana* refers to the hem of a woman's garment.
A plowman [is successful] with a plowman, a washerman with a washerman, and a parrot with a parrot. || 52 ||
*Madhuka* refers to a type of bard, the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha, and a particular bird.
*Madhuka* may refer to *madhuparṇī*; *anu* is used for "inferior" and "subtle" or "small. || 53 ||
Vasuka occurs in śivamallī, arkaparṇa, and romaka.
The word *śiśuka* may refer to a porpoise, as well as to a young child or an owl. || 54 ||
*Kramuka* refers to *paṭṭikālodhra*, *bhadra*, *mustaka*, and *pūga*.
*Karpāsika* refers to the fruit; *kramuka* refers to the *brahmadāru* tree. || 55 ||
There is much [rain] when the sun is in Cancer, and when it is in the Dātyūha or Jalakhātaka [nakṣatras].
*Dhanika* refers to a moneylender among *sādhu*, *dhanya*, *akava*, and *dheṣu*; as for *dhanikā*, it is used in the feminine. || 56 ||
The word *priyaka* refers to the yellow *śāla* tree, the *nīpa* tree, the variegated deer, and the bee.
Kaṅkuma and priyaṅgu; pṛthuka is flattened rice, and śiśu is a child. || 57 ||
The word *yamaka* refers to twin-born beings, a figure of speech in sound (alliteration), and also to self-restraint.
The word *maśaka* is used to denote both a minor disease and a specific type of insect. || 58 ||
*Kulaka* refers to a *paṭola*, a connection between verses, or a cluster (*gucchaka*).
*Kulaka* refers to the best of a family, an anthill, or the *kākatindu* tree. (59)
They call the *tilaka* a spotted deer, and the *tilakālaka* a black spot on the forehead.
It is used in the varieties of coral, in hair, and also in black salt.
*Kulika* may refer to a species of serpent, or to the best of its kind among trees.
*Kuśika* refers to a sage, the residue of oil, the *sarja* tree, and the *akṣa* tree. || 61 ||
*Caṣaka*, however, refers to a drinking vessel for liquor, as well as to types of honey and fish.
*Caṭaka* refers to the sparrow (*kalaviṅka*); *caṭakā* denotes its female and its offspring. || 62 ||
The word *kaṭaka* denotes a bracelet, a mountain ridge, a capital city, and a hip.
[This applies] even to sea salt and to the ivory-tusks of elephants. || 63 ||
Kaṭukā is known as kaṭurohiṇī, and vyoṣa is also considered to be kaṭuka.
*Culuka* is used in the sense of "pouring out" or "a handful"; it is also considered to mean a type of vessel. || 64 ||
*Pulaka* may refer to a species of worm, a cluster [of flowers], the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*), or a defect.
In an elephant's food-ball, in women, in yellow orpiment, and within a stone. || 65 ||
The word *rucaka* refers to an auspicious object, as well as to a neck ornament and ivory.
And in ripe citron, as well as in black salt and viḍaṅga. || 66 ||
And *rucaka* refers to yellow pigment, a horse's ornament, and a garland.
*Kṣuraka* may refer to the *kokilākṣa* plant, the *gokṣura*, or the *tilakadruma* tree. (67)
A lover [rests] upon a blossoming Aśoka tree and an Atimuktaka creeper.
The word *pātuka* may denote one who is prone to falling, as well as a waterfall and an elephant. || 68 ||
He is the sound in the drum, the kettledrum, the war-drum, the small drum, and the thundering cloud.
Āḍhaka is used as a measure of capacity; furthermore, the plant tuvarī is known as āḍhakī. (69)
The *kāraka* is declared to be [the agent] in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), but it is also a *kāraka* in relation to the object (*karman*) and so forth.
The word *cāraka* may denote a keeper of horses and other animals, as well as a spy and a prisoner. (70)
*Tāraka* refers to a helmsman; it also denotes a Daitya, while *tāraka* (neuter) means a star.
In the pupil of the eye, the word *nakṣatra* means "star," as does the word *tārakā*. || 71 ||
The word *vāraka* refers to a horse of a particular breed and also to one who restrains.
And [the term] *jāhaka* is used for a mongoose, a cat, a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), and a water-pot (*aruṇḍikā*). || 72 ||
The word *pāvaka* refers to fire, virtuous conduct, the fire-drill, and the *citrika* plant.
The word *sāyaka* refers to both the bhallātaka and viḍaṅga plants, as well as an arrow and a sword. (73)
*Nāyaka* refers to a leader, one who is preeminent, or even the central gem in a necklace.
The word *prāṇaka* refers to a living being among the class of sentient beings, as well as to the *jīvaka* tree and the *vela* creeper. || 74 ||
The term *jālaka* is said to refer to a bud, while *jālinīphala* refers to a bird's nest.
The word *jālikā* refers to a net, a type of deception, and a kind of garment. (75)
*Bālaka* refers to a child, hair, or the tail of a horse or elephant.
The child [is placed] upon the ring, the hīvera, and the armlet. 76.
The word *vārddhaka* refers to a group of elders, the state of old age, and the activities of the elderly. || 77 ||
The sacrificer is known as Yājini; the sacrificer is Rājakuñjara.
It refers to the seizer in the case of a predatory bird, and to the captor in the case of serpents. || 78 ||
The word *dāraka* refers to a son who causes division; *rātraka* refers to a five-night period.
By him, Vatsara was led to the house of a courtesan and remained there for a night.
*Lāsaka* refers to a dancer, as well as to a peacock; *lāsyakārin* also refers to a dancer.
The word *śārkaka* refers to a lump of sugar and to the froth of milk. || 80 ||
The word *hāraka* refers to a gambler, a thief, prose, discernment, and a breach.
And that which is called *sthāsaka* occurs in the context of ritual worship (*cārccikya*), as well as in a bubble of water and so forth. (81)
*Drāvaka*, however, refers to the splitting of *śilā* (realgar), as well as to one who is cunning or a thief.
*Bhrāmaka* refers to a jackal, a rogue, the sunflower (*sūryāvarta*), and the stone-splitter (*aśmabheda*). || 82 ||
The word *piṇyāka* refers to oil-cake, asafoetida, sesame powder, and saffron.
Pināka refers to the bow of Hara, as well as to a shower of dust and a trident. || 83 ||
The word *kāvṛka* may refer to a cock (*kṛkavāku*), yellow musta-grass (*pītamustaka*), or a ruddy goose (*kokaya*).
*Kṣāraka* refers to a cage for birds, fish, and the like, and also to a net. || 84 ||
The word *pāṭaka* may denote a *mahākiṣku* (a large measure of length) as well as a division of an army and a musical instrument.
In the shaking of dice and the like, and in the increase of capital wealth and the attainment of results; || 85 ||
*Varākaḥ* means "pitiable" or "miserable"; *parākaḥ* refers to a specific penance (*vrata*) or a sword (*khaṅga*).
*Pulāka* may refer to chaff in the case of grain, to a brief summary, or to a grain of boiled rice. (86)
The ripening [of such actions] is proclaimed to be pleasant at first, but in its final transformation, it results in an evil rebirth.
Vipāka refers to ripening, sweating, and also the fruit of unwholesome actions. || 87 ||
*Lampāka* refers to a glutton and a country; *śimphāka* refers to a hoof and a fool.
Sampāka is [a name for] *srkikā* and *dhṛṣṭa*; sampāka is also [a name for] *caturaṅgula*. || 88 ||
The word *mocaka* refers to the plantain tree (*kadalī*), the *śigru* tree, a releaser, and those who are dispassionate.
*Pecaka* refers to the trunk of an elephant and the root of a cat's tail. || 89 ||
*Mecaka* may refer to the eye of a peacock feather (*barhicandra*), and it also denotes the color dark blue or black (*śyāmala*).
But in the case of *timira* (a visual disorder) that is black in color, it should be described as *mecaka*.
*Sūcaka* refers to a needle (an instrument for sewing), a signifier, or a cat.
*Piśuna* refers to a slanderer, a dog, and a crow; *kecaka* refers to a sprinkler and a cloud. || 91 ||
*Locaka* refers to a lump of flesh, the pupil of the eye, and a fingernail.
[It is used] for the forehead ornament of women, and for plantain and indigo cloth. || 92 ||
In the case of "nirbuddhi," "karṇapūra," and "maurvyā," [the elision occurs] when there is a loose leather [band] on the ground.
*Modaka* is to be known as that which causes joy, and *modaka* is a specific kind of edible food. (93)
*Kholaka* refers to a cooking vessel, an anthill, a betel-nut shell, and a head-ornament.
The word *golaka* refers to the son of a widow born from her paramour, while *maṇika* refers to molasses. || 94 ||
*Kūpaka* may mean a rope on a tree, a vessel for oil, or a cavity.
At a well, at a funeral pyre, at a small well, and on a stone in water; 95.
*Kūlaka* refers to a worm and a mountain; *pratīra*, however, also denotes a bank and a funeral mound (*stūpa*).
The learned know *rūpaka* as a drama, a rogue, and a poetic ornament. || 96 ||
*Cṛtaka* refers to a well and also to a mango tree; *sūtaka* refers to both mercury and the birth of a child.
*Lūnaka* refers to a split animal; *śūcaka* refers to a juice in the rainy season. || 97 ||
*Kīcaka* may refer to a type of demon, a withered bamboo, or a particular species of tree.
*Kīṭaka* refers to a species of worm; in other contexts, *kīṭaka* denotes one who is cruel, like the word *kīṭa*. || 98 ||
Jīvaka is found in the *pītaśāla* tree, as well as in the *kṣapaṇa* and *vṛddhajīvina* plants.
[The word] "sevini" [is used] even for a living creature, a snake-charmer, or a tree. || 99 ||
They say that "ājīva" refers to one's livelihood, even when it exists somewhere [only] nominally.
In the context of verbal ornaments, *dīpaka* (the illuminator) refers to that which produces illumination.
The word *cīraka* is considered to mean a contemptuous letter or a document; *cīrikā* is likewise understood in these senses.
The word *sevaka*, however, is used in the sense of a lap (*praseva*) and, like other [words], in the sense of a dependent (*anujīvī*). || 101 ||
*Aśoka* is considered to be *vañjula*, *māna*, and both types of *drumaniḥśoka*.
*Aśoka* is known as *kaṭurohiṇī* (the bitter plant), and it is also remembered for the tree (*pādapa*). || 102 ||
*Āloka* means seeing or light; *āloka* also refers to the recitation of bards.
A *peṭaka* is a collection of books and the like, or a cluster of *pañjūṣaṇas*. (103)
Heraka may refer to a particular Buddha, and also to a member of the Mahākāla host.
The word *dhenuka* is used for the female organ of women and also for a herd of cows.
The term *viveka* may refer to a water tank, as well as to discernment and seclusion.
Gairika refers to the mineral gold; *praseka* means sprinkling, pouring, or falling. || 105 ||

One should know that *vaijika* refers to the marking-nut (*śigru*) oil and the cause of immediate sprouting; *koraka* refers to a bud; and *kakkolaka* refers to both the kakkola berry and the lotus stalk. 106.
The word *kautuka* may signify longing, a festival, sport, or joy.
And in auspiciousness and curiosity handed down through tradition. || 107 ||
It is taught that one should recite [the mantra] during the times of enjoyment, such as when opening the sūtras, singing songs, and so forth.
*Kauśika* refers to a mongoose, a snake-catcher, *guggulu* resin, and *śakra*. (108)
The patronymic Kauśika is derived from Viśvāmitra, Kośāgra, and Ulūka as well.
Kauśikī refers to Caṇḍikā and also to a particular river. || 109 ||
The word *pratīka* is said to mean a limb or part, as well as that which is adverse or contrary.
Bhūtīka is also [known as] bhūnimba, dīpyaka, karpūra, and kattṛṇa. || 110 ||
*Abhīkaḥ* refers to one who is lustful, cruel, wise, or free from fear.
The word *valmīka* refers to an anthill, a type of leprosy, and a sage. (111)
*Anīka* is said to be used in the sense of "dear," while *vyalīka* is recorded as being used in the sense of "citizen" or "townsman."
*Vyalīka* refers to that which is unpleasant, improper action, embarrassment, and affliction. (112)
*Nālīka* refers to a section of an arrow and to a lotus; *nālīka* also denotes an arrow and a thorn.
The word *alīka* is used when something unpleasant is spoken; it is also used for that which is untrue. (113)
He is indeed conformable to his family and his conduct, even in his past life.
*Ulūka* may refer to the *kuruvinda* plant, an owl, or the *pecaka* (a type of bat) that destroys the *jambha* demon. || 114 ||
*Śambūka* refers to the frontal lobe at the end of an elephant's forehead, a type of demon, and a snail.
Bandhūka refers to the bandhujīva flower; bandhūka also denotes the pītaśālaka tree.
They know the word *maṇḍūka* to denote a frog, a kinsman who causes a rift, the *dardura* plant, and the *śoṇaka* tree.
Maṇḍūkī is known as maṇḍūkaparṇī, and varṇaka is recorded as a synonym for āraṇī. || 116 ||
In the case of anointing with sandalwood, there may be a colored ointment; then, a child.
The word *vartaka* refers to a child, a fool, a thin person, and an embryo; it also denotes a horse's hoof and a bird. (117)
Puṣpaka is for diseases of the eyes and affection; Ratnakaṅkaṇa is likewise.
And in the aerial chariot of Kubera, in Kāśīśa, and in Rasāñjana; || 118 ||
In iron, bronze, clay, charcoal, a cart, or even a flower-cart.
Pūrṇaka refers to a golden-crested bird, while Pūrṇikā denotes one whose nose has been cut off.
The word *darśaka* may mean a doorkeeper, one who shows, or one who is skilled.
Padmaka is also [the name for] the wood of the lotus tree and for the *ibhabindu* and *jālaka* varieties. || 120 ||
*Dīpyaka* is a synonym for *ajamodā*, *yavānī*, and *barhicūḍā*.
*Sasyaka* may refer to a gem, a sword, or the interior of a coconut. (121)
The term *raktaka* refers to those who are attached to red garments and withered bandhūka flowers.
